messages.subject: What's a good way to incorporate rounding in measurement in STAN?
parts:
If I have repeated measurements of a binomial proportion, then a natural way to model it would be with something like:

stan_data <- list(
num_obs=3,
y = c(0,0,0.01),
sample_size=c(300,300,300)
)
stan_code <- '
  data {
int num_obs;
    real y[num_obs]; // Observed residuals
int sample_size[num_obs];
  }
  parameters {
real<lower=0,upper=1> p;
  }
  model {
real y_sigma[num_obs];

for(j in 1:num_obs)
y_sigma[j] <- sqrt(p*(1-p)/sample_size[j]);
    y ~normal(p ,y_sigma) ;
  }
'

But how would I modify this code if I knew that the data I was getting was being rounded to the nearest integer percentage?

That won't work as written, because yact is unconstrained, but
has support only on y +/- 0.005.

If you want to treat the true value as missing data and assume
the measurement error is uniform, you could do this so that
the support matches the constraints (the uniform on y_err is
implicit):

data {
...
vector[N] y_obs;
}
parameters {
...
vector<lower=-0.005, upper=0.005>[N] y_err;
}
transformed parameters {
...
vector[N] y;
...
y <- y_obs + y_err;
}
model {
...
y ~ normal(mu_y, sigma_y);
}

where y_meas is the measurement of y.

This is another case where the parser's going to spit out
a Jacobian warning that you don't need to worry about.

But there may be rounding error plus measurement error, in which case,
it might make sense to just roll the rounding error in with the rest of
the error and not try to build an explicit measurement error model.

- Bob

And then z gets modeled with truncation, so you need to use the truncated normal distribution or whatever.

No need to assume that the measurement error is uniform. What’s happening is that the measurement is giving you truncation information.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] What's a good way to incorporate rounding in measurement in STAN?
parts:
Stan assumes support on the constrained parameter space. That
is, everywhere the parameter meets its constraints, it should
have density > 0.

If that is violated, then multiple things might happen. In the
best case, you'll init near the solution and the sampler won't
move near the boundaries. If you had a big vector of y ~ uniform(-1,1)
and used our random inits, you're very unlikely to be able to move.

Michael will have to weigh in on what happens with bias in cases
where things run without crashing or getting stuck.

- Bob

On Friday, August 21, 2015 at 2:45:55 PM UTC-7, Andrew Gelman wrote:
Bob:  No, I don’t think your model is correct.  Rounding to 2 decimal places is not the same as adding independent uniform(-.005,.005) errors.  In practice, the two approaches might give similar results—and I’m pretty sure Bob’s will run faster, as it doesn’t require normal cdfs—but it’s not the same model.  I guess if anyone wanted, they could run a simulation study to see if the two approaches are the same in practice.
A

It's not (necessarily, obviously) the same model, but I wouldn't say it "isn't correct".

we have p, the unknown proportion, and y, the observed, rounded value. Given that y is rounded, we know that it can't be more than 0.005 away from y_true, which is unobserved.

so:

ydelta ~ uniform(-0.005, 0.005); // specifies prior information for an unobserved parameter, the distance from the rounded data to the actual value

y_true <- y + ydelta;

y_true ~ normal(foo,bar); // the jacobian warning will show up here, since y_true is a transformed parameter

however, because of the normal distribution's symmetry, this can be rewritten:

y ~ normal(foo - ydelta,bar); // this doesn't trigger the jacobian warning and looks more like a likelihood

this whole thing works really because the normal density is determined by the difference between two values, or looked at another way because it's symmetric between the first and second argument. We had a big discussion on this that I started recently (see post about jacobian errors).

so, another way to look at this model is where we assume a prior for the rounding error to be uniform, and do inference on the posterior of the true value under that assumption. You could actually work with other priors, but if you know only that the rounding error is inside an interval, the uniform prior is the maximum entropy one.

Stan assumes support on the constrained parameter space.  That
is, everywhere the parameter meets its constraints, it should
have density > 0.

can it throw warnings when this is violated? that should be relatively easy to check for at least a lot of simple cases, such as if you have a statement:

y ~ foo(bar,baz)

where y is a parameter, not a transformed parameter or an expression, and bar, baz, etc are constants, and foo is known to have support on some region, and y is not constrained to that region.

for example

real y;

y ~ exponential(1/100);

etc.

If that is violated, then multiple things might happen.  In the
best case, you'll init near the solution and the sampler won't
move near the boundaries.  If you had a big vector of y ~ uniform(-1,1)
and used our random inits, you're very unlikely to be able to move.

Michael will have to weigh in on what happens with bias in cases
where things run without crashing or getting stuck.

which looks the same to me, only it's going to be harder to code in Stan.

here.  Or are you saying we should use something other than a uniform rounding

Bob, I'm pretty sure Andrew is saying that the rounding means that whatever your model is for the "true" measurement error, the fact that it's rounded means that conditional on the observed value, you have to use a truncated form of your measurement error distribution, truncated to the region that makes sense given the rounding.

if y is observed, and y_err is a measurement error, and you have a model for your measurement error

y_err ~ foodistrib(a,b,c,d,e)

then consistent with the information we have, we have to truncate this prior to the region y-0.005 to y+0.005

in pseudocode, since I am not sure how stan does truncation:

y_err ~ foodistrib(a,b,c,d,e) Truncated_to(y-0.005,y+0.005)

This, more or less, provides a mixture of likelihood and prior information, and I think it more or less is equivalent to Michael Betancourt's model. I think it's a bit ... awkward. and the justification for my model above, using maximum entropy priors on an unobserved rounding error seems more, at least understandable.

I take it back. It looks like what Andrew and Michael are proposing is to actually discretize the likelihood model on the grid of possible rounded outcomes, and then calculate a likelihood as a probability to get the actual discrete y_obs value. Is that fair to say?

I don't think this discrete model is a problem for Stan to sample since it's in the likelihood, and it's still a continuous function of the parameters.

Still, I think the motivation for my model involving a uniform prior on the rounding portion of the error also logically holds, it doesn't ONLY hold when the data were sampled uniformly, since the posterior for the y_err values need not be uniform!

In my/bob's case, you're writing the likelihood:

OK, here's the result of coding Andrew's approach and my approach
(which I believe is the same as Daniel Lakeland's modulo the Stan
coding), for the BDA3 exercise 3.5. I have some questions below
about fitting the measurement error as a parameter and the relation to cut.

For those without BDA3, the problem Andrew's referring to is this,
without the extra bits:

Question
--------
3.5 ... Suppose we weigh an object five times and
measure weights, rounded to the nearest pound, of 10, 10, 12,
11, 9. Assume the unrounded measurements are normally distributed
with a noninformative prior distribution on mu and sigma^2.

b) Give the correct posterior distribution for (mu, sigma^2)
treating the measurements as rounded.

Answer
------
Andrew's answer from his answer key corresponds to the following Stan model:

transformed data {
int<lower=0> N;
vector[5] y;
N <- 5;
y[1] <- 10;
y[2] <- 10;
y[3] <- 12;
y[4] <- 11;
y[5] <- 9;
}
parameters {
real mu;
real<lower=0> sigma_sq;
}
transformed parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma;
sigma <- sqrt(sigma_sq);
}
model {
increment_log_prob(-2 * log(sigma));
for (n in 1:N)
increment_log_prob(log(Phi((y[n] + 0.5 - mu) / sigma)
- Phi((y[n] - 0.5 - mu) / sigma)));
}


What I was proposing corresponds to this model:

transformed data {
int<lower=0> N;
vector[5] y;
N <- 5;
y[1] <- 10;
y[2] <- 10;
y[3] <- 12;
y[4] <- 11;
y[5] <- 9;
}
parameters {
real mu;
real<lower=0> sigma_sq;
vector<lower=-0.5, upper=0.5>[5] y_err;
}
transformed parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma;
sigma <- sqrt(sigma_sq);
}
model {
increment_log_prob(-2 * log(sigma));
for (n in 1:N)
(y + y_err) ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}


Here's what Stan says.

Andrew's model:

sigma 1.35 0.03 0.72 0.63 0.92 1.17 1.57 3.06 739 1.01
lp__ -8.36 0.04 1.16 -11.55 -8.78 -8.01 -7.54 -7.22 685 1.00


My model:

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
mu 10.42 0.00 0.19 10.06 10.30 10.42 10.55 10.79 2324 1
sigma_sq 0.63 0.01 0.23 0.32 0.47 0.59 0.75 1.20 2099 1
y_err[1] 0.19 0.00 0.23 -0.35 0.05 0.24 0.38 0.49 2740 1
y_err[2] 0.19 0.00 0.23 -0.36 0.06 0.23 0.37 0.49 2755 1
y_err[3] -0.40 0.00 0.11 -0.50 -0.47 -0.43 -0.36 -0.09 2694 1
y_err[4] -0.24 0.00 0.21 -0.49 -0.41 -0.29 -0.13 0.27 2874 1
y_err[5] 0.39 0.00 0.12 0.07 0.34 0.42 0.47 0.50 2593 1
sigma 0.79 0.00 0.14 0.57 0.69 0.77 0.87 1.09 2110 1

interval on mu and for sigma.

y_obs <- round(y)
y_err <- y_obs - round(y)

But clearly my model's not doing that, because I see how Andrew's model fits
that generative story.

like this treating the measurement error as an unknown parameter? I believe
this is related to the suggested use of cut in the BUGS Book, but given that
I only have a print version, I don't have it with me on the road (it's around
page 202 from the Amazon search, but most of the analysis isn't part of
the preview).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] What's a good way to incorporate rounding in measurement in STAN?
parts:
D'oh! I can answer my own question from first principles. All I
had to do was step away from the computer.

Punchline: Marginalizing the latent error parameters out of my model
gives you Andrew's model.


Posterior for Andrew's model:

p_a(mu, sigma | y)

propto (1 / sigma^2) PROD_n normal_cdf(y + 0.5 | mu, sigma) - normal_cdf(y - 0.5 | mu, sigma)

= (1 /sigma^2) PROD_n INT_{z in (y - 0.5, y + 0.5)} normal(z | mu, sigma)


Posterior for my model:

p_b(mu, sigma, y_err | y)

propto p(mu, sigma) p(y_err) p(y_err + y | mu, sigma)

propto (1 / sigma^2) PROD_n normal(y + y_err | mu, sigma)


The trick is thinking of the generative model as producing
a "true" measurement z by

z ~ normal(mu, sigma)

and then defining two (deterministic) functions of z by

y <- round(z)

y_err <- z - y

Then we observe y and estimate z as (y + y_err). Then we
get

p(y_err) = uniform(-0.5, 0.5)

Note that this is not generating y_err --- it's just providing the
density of the random variable y_err, which is derived as a function
of z, where z does does have a generative story. Whew --- that was a
challenge for me to write out and I'm still not sure I've convinced
myself of that last bit other than that the math works out in the next step.

Now if you marginalize the y_err out of my model, you get Andrew's model:

p_b(mu, sigma | y)

= p(mu, sigma) * p(y | mu, sigma)

= p(mu, sigma) * PROD_n p(y[n] | mu, sigma)

propto (1 / sigma^2) PROD_n INT_{y_err in (-0.5, 0.5)} p(y_err) p(y[n] + y_err | mu, sigma)

= (1 / sigma^2) PROD_n INT_{z in (y - 0.5, y + 0.5)} p(z | mu, sigma)

This assumes the distribution of y_err to be uniform(-0.5, 0.5).

Andrew basically followed up with the same examples.

- Bob

On Saturday, August 22, 2015 at 12:31:58 AM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
D'oh!  I can answer my own question from first principles.  All I
had to do was step away from the computer.

I know that feeling. Thanks for giving the analysis. I think your analysis confirms my story that

A) your model isn't wrong, it's just a model for both the underlying "true" measurement error, and the individual roundoffs

B) generative models aren't the only way to think about writing Stan programs (this goes back to my post on Jacobians and the meaning of ~ in Stan), as you point out, p(y_err) isn't generating y_err because y_err is a deterministic function of y and z, the underlying normal. I consider p(y_err) to be a maxent prior on y_err, but in your math the uniform is necessary to that you can get a correspondence between the marginalization, and the model that Andrew used with the normal_cdf. There are different perspectives here, but they lead to the same conclusion.

Punchline:  Marginalizing the latent error parameters out of my model
gives you Andrew's model.

As a general perspective, my intuition is that it should always work out to write something of the form:

an_expression_involving_something_you_know_or_want_to_know ~ a_distribution_describing_your_state_of_knowledge(parameters, describing, knowledge)

Rarely are we in the situation where the frequency distribution assumed is actually "true". So for example in Andrew's example you have a scale, and you assume if you put a weight on it, it generates say a voltage that is normally distributed, and then rounds off the measurement of the voltage.

But, why normally distributed? In reality, it's probably not, it's gotta be much lighter-tailed than that (ie. it has to have finite bounds based on the voltage available in the battery or whatnot) yet within those bounds it could be normal, or t, or even some kind of skewed distribution, or it could vary from time to time based on the temperature of the transistors... etc

So, it's not necessary to get too attached to the idea that "generative" models are the one-true-path for modeling. For example, it leads to intuitions like that uniform distributions will only work if the distribution of the actual roundoffs is uniform.

parts:
On Saturday, August 22, 2015 at 11:50:15 AM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
What the math showed is that Andrew's model produces the same
result as marginalizing out the latent parameters from my model.

The story with the latent variables is generative.  Generate
a measurement, then round it off.  That measurement model
doesn't need to be normal, but that's a good generic assumption
for effects that are additive combinations of other effects.

The uniform "prior" on p(y_err) is just derived from working
backward from the measurement model (normal error plus rounding).
That was the whole point of Andrew's exercise in BDA.

The exercise of course has a particular "generative" model from the start. But the original question was "how to include roundoff in a binomial proportion reported as rounded to the nearest percent" and the thought process that brought me to my model for that was: "we know the rounding means that the underlying value was within a particular interval, so put a maxent prior on that difference value and then subtract it from the measurement and tell Stan that you know the distribution of this new quantity which is a function of data and parameter"

I feel like that's a different route to the model than thinking the other way around, and the math showed that it was marginally, the same in your case. One question is, is this model building methodology valid in general? Can you put distributions over f(data,parameters) by claiming from your scientific knowledge that such a distribution is justified, and always produce a model which is mathematically well posed (not necessarily maximally efficient, or maximally informative mind you, but at least which produces a normalizable posterior pdf for example)?

I don't think we'll get a solution to that question, except that most likely there are some counterexamples where the method produces bad results because of pathologies in the function f, or whatnot.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] What's a good way to incorporate rounding in measurement in STAN?
parts: > The exercise of course has a particular "generative" model from the start. But the original question was "how to include roundoff in a binomial proportion reported as rounded to the nearest percent" and the thought process that brought me to my model for that was: "we know the rounding means that the underlying value was within a particular interval, so put a maxent prior on that difference value and then subtract it from the measurement and tell Stan that you know the distribution of this new quantity which is a function of data and parameter"

No, no, no, no. Unless the distribution of the latent measurement is
uniform, this “maxent” distribution will be inconsistent with the rest
of the measurement model and define only a weird target distribution.
In particular, the rounding is a censoring process which belongs in
the _likelihood_ and has nothing to do with _priors_.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] What's a good way to incorporate rounding in measurement in STAN?
parts:
I'm particularly interested in this topic because I think it's frequently the case that a model is more naturally expressed (for me) in this way.

For example, suppose you have an A/D converter looking at a signal which is composed of f(t) whose form you know, plus a bunch of high frequency noise which has MSE sigma which you know approximately and this high frequency noise can be considered gaussian like, plus some low frequency noise which has total amplitude less than epsilon, and of course, roundoff error in the A/D... (let's pretend this is to nearest 0.001)

You have NO idea what the frequency distribution of the values caused by the low frequency signal will be, but you know the error they induce is always between -epsilon and epsilon.

To me, a very natural model for this is:

y_round ~ uniform(-0.001,0.001);
y_err ~ uniform(-epsilon,epsilon);
sigma ~ exponential(1/my_guess_for_sigma); // or maybe some other prior expressing what I know about sigma
Data - y_err -y_round ~ normal(f(t), sigma)

especially if I want to know something about the low frequency signal y_err which is polluting my measurements...

Very often, it's latent things like measurement errors or diffusion coefficients, or the size of the effect of some temperature change... or whatever that I'd like to know. It makes sense to write models that directly do inference via a parameter on the thing I'm interested in.

messages.author: 37f85c6188fe5eeb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] What's a good way to incorporate rounding in measurement in STAN?
parts:
Another example, suppose it's just like Andrew's example, but someone designing the microcontroller code for the scale had a bug, so 50 % of the time the display rounds to the nearest 1 lb, 40% of the time it rounds UP, and 10% of the time it rounds DOWN.

Now, you could put a maxent prior on the roundoff errors that's a mixture model of the 3 possibilities, and that would be a step-function, but of course HMC isn't going to like that. So you could graph this step function and design a sort of smoothish approximation to that step function, and then write

for(i in 1:N)
  increment_log_prob(my_smooth_approximation(roundoff_parameter[i]));

Or you could write a weird likelihood, and try to back-out the rounding errors with weird generated quantities...

Generally, it makes sense to me to write your model so you have parameters that describe the unknown quantities of interest, and priors on those parameters that describe the information you have about them going into the analysis.

I don’t have the energy for any more discussion of this, but let me just echo Betancourt:  It does not make sense to think of there being a “prior” on the errors.  What we have is a data model, giving the data as a function of the unobserved continuous measurement.  In one of the models I posted yesterday, I did express things in terms of a prior for the roundoff error, but that is truly a hack and not a good way to write this sort of model.  In general, and as usual, it is best to write the model directly as I did in my model rounding_latent_2.stan.  Here I speak, not of Stan efficiency, but of general statistical principles.
